title: CDL General Knowledge
summary: The core rules every commercial driver must know: licensing, inspection, safe control, hazards, emergencies and cargo.

blocks.text: Federal rules set the minimum. Some states require a CDL for more vehicles, but none require less.

rows: Any combination with a GCWR of 26,001 lbs or more, when the towed unit's GVWR is over 10,000 lbs. Example: a 14,000-lb pickup towing a 14,000-lb trailer (28,000 lbs total).
A single vehicle of 26,001 lbs GVWR or more, or one towing a unit of 10,000 lbs GVWR or less. Example: a 30,000-lb truck towing an 8,000-lb trailer.
A smaller vehicle that is designed to carry 16 or more people (counting the driver), or that needs hazmat placards.
Tank vehicle plus hazardous materials (N + H)

items: Only the P, S and N endorsements can go on a Commercial Learner's Permit (CLP). H and T cannot.
The skills test has three parts, taken in order: vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, and the on-road test.
You may hold only one driver license, from your home state. A court can fine you up to $5,000 or jail you, and all states share a computer system to catch extra licenses.
Tell your employer within 30 days about any traffic conviction except parking, in any vehicle, even your own car.
Tell your employer within 2 business days if your license is suspended, revoked or canceled, or if you are disqualified.
When you apply for a driving job, list every driving job you held in the past 10 years.

rows: 0.04% BAC or more (and other major offenses)
At least 1 year for a first offense; 3 years if the CMV was placarded for hazmat; life for a second offense
Using a CMV for a felony involving controlled substances
Life, even on the first offense
3 or more serious violations in 3 years
1st: 60 days. 2nd in 3 years: 120 days. 3rd in 3 years: 1 year

blocks.text: Serious traffic violations include excessive speeding (15 mph or more over the posted limit), reckless driving, improper or erratic lane changes, following too closely, and driving a CMV without a CDL, the right class or the needed endorsements. Hand-held phone and texting convictions in a CMV carry the same 60-day and 120-day disqualifications.
Safety is the most important reason to inspect. If a federal or state inspector finds your vehicle unsafe, it is put out of service until it is fixed.

rows: At least 4/32 inch in every major groove
No recapped, retreaded or re-grooved tires
No welding repairs, missing clamps, studs or lugs, or bent or cracked lock rings
No more than 10 degrees (about 2 inches at the rim of a 20-inch wheel)
Out of service if one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing
No leaks or breaks; leaks can let carbon monoxide into the cab or sleeper

items: After a tire change, stop a short while later and re-check the wheel nuts.

Required emergency equipment: a fire extinguisher, spare fuses (unless you have circuit breakers), and warning devices. Warning devices can be three red reflective triangles, at least six fuses, or three liquid-burning flares.
If you carry hazardous materials, also check for proper shipping papers and placards.
Review the last driver's inspection report. You sign it only if defects were listed and certified as repaired or not needed.
Before checking the engine compartment, make sure the parking brake is set and/or the wheels are chocked.

rows: Comes on, then goes off. If it stays on, ABS is not working.
Up to normal within seconds of starting
50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes, then on to governor cut-out (usually about 120 to 140 psi). Dual air systems: 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds (see the Air Brakes lesson).

items: Hydraulic brakes: pump the pedal 3 times, then hold firm pressure for 5 seconds. The pedal should not move.
Parking brake: set it, put the vehicle in a low gear, and gently pull forward against it. It should hold.
Service brakes: move forward at about 5 mph and push the brake pedal firmly. Pulling to one side, an odd pedal feel or a delayed stop can mean brake trouble.

blocks.text: On the road, check cargo securement within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles (whichever comes first), and after every break. If you see, hear, smell or feel anything odd, stop safely and check it out.

items: Manual transmission: partly engage the clutch before taking your right foot off the brake, so you don't roll back.
If the drive wheels spin, take your foot off the accelerator.
Hold the wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides.

Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized transmissions need double clutching. If you miss a gear, don't force it: return to neutral, release the clutch, match engine speed to road speed, and try again.
Downshift before you enter a curve. On an automatic, choose a low range on downgrades for more engine braking.
A retarder slows you and saves brake wear, but turn it off on wet, icy or snowy roads; it can make the drive wheels skid.

blocks.text: Backing is always dangerous because you cannot see everything behind you. Avoid it when you can. When you must back, back toward the driver's side, use a helper, and agree on hand signals, especially the one for stop.

items: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead: about one block in town, about a quarter mile on the highway.
A light that has been green a long time will likely change. Slow down and be ready to stop.
Adjust mirrors before each trip, with the trailer straight. Each mirror should show part of your own vehicle.
Convex mirrors show more, but things look smaller and farther away than they are.
When changing lanes, check mirrors before, after signaling, after starting the move, and after finishing.

blocks.caption: A light that has been green for a long time will probably change before you get there. Start slowing and be ready to stop.

items: Signal early, signal the whole way through the turn, and cancel the signal afterward.
Warn drivers behind you that you're slowing by lightly tapping the brake pedal to flash the brake lights.
Don't wave other drivers on to pass. You could cause a crash and be blamed.
At dawn, dusk, or in rain or snow, use low-beam headlights, not just clearance lights.

blocks.text: If you stop on the road or shoulder, turn on your four-way flashers and put out warning devices within 10 minutes. Don't rely on taillights; drivers have hit parked trucks thinking they were moving.

rows: 10, 100 and 200 feet back toward approaching traffic
One within 10 feet of the front or rear corner, one about 100 feet behind, one about 100 feet ahead
Hill, curve or other blocked view
If a hill, curve or other obstruction keeps drivers from seeing your vehicle within 500 feet, move the rearmost device back down the road (up to 500 feet) so they get a warning in time.

blocks.text: Carry the triangles between you and oncoming traffic as you walk, so drivers can see you.
Total stopping distance = perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance. An alert driver takes about 1¾ seconds to perceive a hazard, plus ¾ to 1 second to react.

items: Double your speed (20 to 40 mph) and impact and braking distance grow about 4 times. At 60 mph it's 9 times; at 80 mph, 16 times.
An empty truck usually needs more distance to stop than a loaded one because it has less traction.
Wet roads can double stopping distance.

rows: Slow down about one-third (55 to about 35 mph)
Slow down by half or more

items: Bridges freeze before the road. Watch closely when it is near 32°F.
Black ice is a thin, clear layer that makes the road look wet. Ice that is starting to melt is the most slippery.
To check for ice, feel the mirror, mirror support or antenna. No spray from other vehicles on a wet-looking road also means ice.
Hydroplaning can start as low as 30 mph. Release the accelerator and push in the clutch; don't brake.
Trucks with a high center of gravity can roll over at a curve's posted speed. Slow down before the curve, not in it.

blocks.caption: A curve warning: slow down before you enter, then use slight power through the curve.

blocks.text: Speeding traffic is the number one cause of injuries and deaths in work zones. Obey work zone limits, and slow down even more when workers are close to the road.
The space ahead is the most important space. Trucks and buses most often hit the vehicle in front of them, usually from following too closely.

rows: 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length

items: Measure it by counting seconds from when the vehicle ahead passes a landmark until you reach it.
If someone tailgates you, increase your following distance. Don't speed up or flash your brake lights.
In heavy traffic, the safest speed is the speed of other traffic, if it is legal and safe.
A loaded truck accelerates slowly, so you need a much larger gap to enter or cross traffic.
If a heavy load slows you on an upgrade, stay in the right lane.
Strong winds make it hard to stay in your lane, especially coming out of tunnels. Avoid driving alongside others.

blocks.caption: If a heavy load slows you, especially on an upgrade, stay in the right lane so faster traffic can get by.

items: Don't trust posted bridge heights. Re-paving or packed snow can reduce clearance.
An empty van rides higher than a loaded one. Clearing a bridge loaded doesn't mean you'll clear it empty.
If the road tilts your truck toward signs or trees at the edge, drive a little closer to the center.

rows: Turn wide as you finish the turn, and keep the rear close to the curb so no one can pass on your right.
Give oncoming cars room to pass or stop. Don't back up; you might hit someone behind you.
Reach the center of the intersection before turning, because the rear wheels off-track.

blocks.text: A hazard is any road condition or road user that is a possible danger. It becomes an emergency when it actually blocks you, such as a confused driver who suddenly cuts in front of you. Spotting hazards early gives you time to act.

items: Downhill off-ramps that also turn are dangerous: it's hard to slow, and braking while turning is risky. Posted ramp speeds may suit cars, not trucks.
If you can see a vehicle but not its driver, the driver can't see you.
Impaired-driver clues: weaving, leaving the road, stopping at odd times, sudden speed changes, an open window in cold weather.
Motorcyclists and bicyclists give the clearest head and body clues before they turn.
An ice cream truck means children may be nearby and may not see you.

blocks.caption: Slow-moving vehicle emblem: a red triangle with an orange center, used on farm and construction equipment.

blocks.text: A distraction is anything that takes your attention off driving. Hands-free phones distract you just as much as hand-held ones.

items: Federal rule: no holding a phone for a call, no dialing by pressing more than one button, and no reaching so far that you leave your seated, belted position.
Texting means manually typing or reading text on a device, including e-mail, messages and web pages.
The only exception is contacting police or emergency services in an emergency.
Phone or texting violations: 60 days for a 2nd offense in 3 years, 120 days for 3 or more.
Texting raises the odds of a safety-critical event about 23 times. Dialing raises them about 6 times.
A text takes your eyes away about 4.6 seconds: roughly 371 feet, a football field, at 55 mph.
Aggressive driving is selfish and pushy. Road rage means trying to harm or assault someone.
If an aggressive driver targets you, first get out of their way. Avoid eye contact and ignore gestures.
If you later see that driver crash, stop a safe distance away, wait for police, and report what you saw.

rows: The only safe cure is sleep. Stop for the night or take a 15 to 20 minute nap.
Take breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours
Many heavy-vehicle crashes happen between midnight and 6 a.m. Driving mid-afternoon or when you would normally be asleep is also risky.
Only time sobers you. The liver handles about one-third ounce per hour.
12 oz of 5% beer = 5 oz of 12% wine = 1½ oz of 80-proof liquor
Allowed on duty only if a doctor says they won't affect safe driving
Don't drive if too ill; in an emergency, drive only to the nearest safe place
See about 350 to 500 feet; use them when safe and legal, and dim before they glare
May give only half their light
2 seconds of glare blindness at 55 mph is more than half a football field

blocks.caption: When bright lights come toward you, look slightly right at the lane or edge line.

items: If your license requires glasses or contacts, keep a spare set in the vehicle.

Fog: best not to drive at all; wait at a rest area or truck stop. If you must, slow down before you enter it, use low beams and fog lights even by day, and turn on your four-way flashers. Taillights ahead may belong to a vehicle that has left the road, so use roadside reflectors to follow the curve.
Winter: clear ice from radiator shutters and don't close the winterfront too tightly, or the engine may overheat. Carry enough chains and extra cross-links that fit your drive tires.
Exhaust leaks are extra dangerous in winter with the windows closed.
Deep water: slow down, use a low gear, keep light brake pressure and raise rpm. After, keep light pressure a short distance to dry the brakes, then make a test stop.
Hot weather: inspect tires every 2 hours or 100 miles. Don't let air out of hot tires. If a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools.
Only remove a radiator cap once the system has cooled enough to touch the cap bare-handed.
Bleeding tar rises to the surface in hot weather and is very slippery.

blocks.text: Expect a train at every crossing. The round yellow advance warning sign means slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop.

items: The crossbuck means yield to trains. A sign below it shows the number of tracks.
If you must stop and there is no stop line, stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.
At gates, wait until the gates are up and the lights stop flashing.
On multiple tracks, a passing train can hide a second one. Look again before crossing.
A tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear one track, more than 15 for two.
Never shift gears while crossing. Be sure you can get all the way across before you start.
Lowboys, car carriers, moving vans and possum-belly trailers can get stuck on raised crossings.
If you get stuck, get out and away from the tracks, then call the number posted (give the DOT number if shown) or 911.
Brake fade: hot brakes need more and more pressure to slow you, until they may not stop you at all.
Shift into a low gear before starting down a grade. Modern trucks have less drag, so you may need a lower gear going down than going up.
Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share, so the others overheat and fade.
Escape ramps use soft, loose material to stop runaway trucks. If your brakes fail on a downgrade, use one.
Get into the proper low gear.
When you reach your safe speed (say 40 mph), brake hard enough to feel a definite slowdown.
Release when you are about 5 mph under it (35 mph). Each application takes about 3 seconds.
Repeat each time you reach the safe speed.
You can almost always turn to miss something faster than you can stop. Don't brake while turning, and counter-steer once you pass the obstacle.
If a driver drifts into your lane, steer right. If all sides are blocked, right is usually best.
If you must leave the road, don't brake until you are under about 20 mph, then brake gently. To return, turn sharply back on, then counter-steer as one move.
Controlled braking: brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with small steering moves.

Stab braking: brake fully, release when the wheels lock, and re-apply fully as soon as they roll again. It can take up to 1 second for them to start rolling; re-apply too soon and the vehicle won't straighten out.
Hydraulic brake failure: downshift, pump the pedal, and use the parking brake while holding its release so you can control it.
Heavy steering usually means a front tire failed. After a blowout, hold the wheel firmly, stay off the brakes until you slow, then brake gently. Check all tires once stopped.

rows: Works only when wheels are about to lock. Helps you keep control and steer; may not shorten stopping distance.
Air-braked tractors built on or after March 1, 1997; other air-braked vehicles from March 1, 1998; hydraulic trucks and buses 10,000 lbs GVWR+ from March 1, 1999
Yellow. On trailers: left side, front or rear corner. Some older systems stay lit until over 5 mph.
Brake as usual. Full braking in an emergency is OK only with working ABS on all axles.
Watch for trailer swing-out and ease off if safe
You still have normal brakes. Get it serviced soon.
Skids from spinning drive wheels or turning too fast

items: Most serious skids come from driving too fast for conditions.
The most common skid is a drive-wheel skid. If caused by acceleration, ease off the gas (push in the clutch if very slippery). If caused by braking, stop braking and be ready to counter-steer.
In a front-wheel skid the front goes straight no matter how you steer. The only fix is to let the vehicle slow: stop turning and braking so hard.
At any crash: protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
If helping at someone else's crash, park away from it and use flashers and triangles.
If you have a phone or CB, call for help before getting out.
Move a badly injured person only if fire or traffic makes it necessary. Stop bleeding with direct pressure and keep the person warm.
Under-inflated tires and touching duals can cause tire fires.
If on fire, stop in an open area away from buildings and brush, not at a service station.
Engine fire: turn off the engine and avoid opening the hood. Spray through louvers, the radiator, or from underneath.
Cargo fire in a box trailer: keep the doors shut to limit oxygen.
Aim the extinguisher at the base of the fire and keep going until the material has cooled.
B:C extinguishers handle electrical fires and burning liquids. Class D fires are burning metals.
Never use water on a gasoline fire (it spreads) or an electrical fire. A burning tire needs lots of water to cool it.

blocks.text: You are responsible for inspecting your cargo, spotting overloads and poor balance, and knowing it is secured, even if someone else loaded it.

rows: The maker's loaded weight rating for a single vehicle
Maximum safe weight at a set pressure, printed on the tire's side
Allows less weight on axles that are closer together
Hurts steering, braking and speed control
Too much weight on steering axle
Hard steering and damage to the axle and tires
Too little weight on drive axles
Poor traction; drive wheels may spin

items: Keep cargo low, with the heaviest items under the lightest, to reduce rollover risk.
Blocking fits snugly against the cargo and is secured to the deck. Bracing runs from the upper part of the cargo to the floor or walls.
Tie-downs together must have a working load limit of at least half the cargo's weight.
Use at least 2 tie-downs on any cargo, and at least 1 for every 10 feet (a 30-foot load needs at least 3).
A header board (headache rack) protects you from cargo moving forward.
Cover cargo to protect people from spills and the cargo from weather.
You can't inspect a sealed load, but check that you're within gross and axle weight limits.
Hanging meat is unstable with a high center of gravity. Go slowly on sharp curves and ramps.
With a partial load of livestock, use false bulkheads to keep the animals bunched.
Over-length, over-width or overweight loads need special transit permits.

blocks.text: Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety and property during transport.

items: You need the hazmat endorsement only when the load requires placards.
A tank endorsement is needed for tanks over 119 gallons each that total 1,000 gallons or more, hazardous or not.
While driving, keep shipping papers in a pouch on your door or in clear view within reach. When you leave the cab, put them on the driver's seat.
A placarded vehicle shows at least four identical placards: front, rear and both sides.
Identification numbers are four digits after "UN" or "NA". The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) lists them.
Class 3 is flammable liquids, such as gasoline and acetone.

keyPoints: A CDL is needed at 26,001 lbs GVWR or for 16+ passengers; the CMV alcohol limit is 0.04%, and any alcohol means 24 hours out of service.
Front tires need 4/32 inch of tread, others 2/32; put warning devices out within 10 minutes.
Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead and keep 1 second per 10 feet of length, plus 1 second above 40 mph.
Stopping from 55 mph takes about 419 feet; slow by a third on wet roads and by half on packed snow.
Never hold a phone or text while driving a CMV; hands-free still distracts.
On downgrades, use a low gear and brake from your safe speed down about 5 mph, about 3 seconds each time.
Expect a train at every crossing, and never shift gears on the tracks.
Check cargo within 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles and after every break.
